applied: explain.text: "Kept fully on or fully off" and "more heat than it can shed" are stated of every power transistor, but linear regulators and amplifiers run them half on by design; the current is not "forced to stop" (the switch tries, then breaks down); a MOSFET gate leaks a little; a reversed freewheeling diode …

practice.text: The freewheeling-diode step does not say which way round: fitted the other way it shorts the supply each time the switch turns on. The rule of thumb is more general than the narrowed explanation, as linear regulators and amplifiers run power transistors half on.

interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Screen 7 says a MOSFET gate draws current "only" while changing over (it leaks a tiny amount); screens 11 and 12 say the coil current "is forced" to zero in 0.5 µs, but with no diode the switch only tries to, and breaks down as its voltage soars.
notes: explain.text: "Both give the load about 300 V on average" is true, but into a resistor half-time chopping delivers about twice the power of half on (about 6 kW against 3 kW). At equal load power, about 25% on, switching still makes only about 30 W at 10 kHz, so the point stands; the frozen 75-times figure rests …

sources[1]: The 0.7 V freewheeling drop is the sourced small-signal silicon value; a power diode carrying about 20 A usually drops nearer 1 to 1.5 V. It only moves the 601 V figure by a volt or so, and the course uses 0.7 V throughout.
